image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #974: The General Problem

titleText.es: He descubierto que cuando alguien se toma su tiempo para hacer algo bien en el presente, entonces es un perfeccionista sin capacidad para establecer un orden de prioridades. Sin embargo, cuando alguien se tomó su tiempo para hacer algo bien en el pasado, entonces es un maestro artesano con gran capacidad de predicción.
titleText.en: I find that when someone's taking time to do something right in the present, they're a perfectionist with no ability to prioritize, whereas when someone took time to do something right in the past, they're a master artisan of great foresight.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official English title attributes are preserved exactly. Vision sorted the upper-right reply before the opening request, omitted the accent in SÉ and AHORRARÁ, read LA as A, read 20 as 2O, and split the printed wrap joins DESA-/RROLLANDO and CONDI-/MENTOS.

applications.explanationEn: The rising question frame turns the present form pasas into a polite yes-or-no request.
Me identifies the recipient, pasas gives the handing action, and la sal names the object being passed.
He is the present helper for the speaker, and dicho is the irregular completed-action form of decir.

regions.labelEs: ¡YA LO SÉ! ESTOY DESARROLLANDO UN SISTEMA PARA PASARTE CONDIMENTOS ARBITRARIOS.

applications.explanationEn: Lo stands before sé and supplies the direct object ‘it.’
Estoy supplies the ongoing present frame, and desarrollando names the activity in progress.
Para introduces the purpose, and pasarte remains an unchanged infinitive with te attached.
Te attaches to pasar to identify one familiar listener as the recipient.
Pasarte combines the handing action with its recipient, and condimentos names what is passed.
Arbitrarios follows the noun because it describes which kinds of condiments the system can handle.
Both words are masculine plural, so the adjective ends in -os.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed quantity is an Arabic numeral rather than a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Han is the plural present helper, and pasado supplies the completed form of pasar.
Han pasado gives the elapsed-time verb frame, and minutos names the unit of the excluded quantity.
The three fixed words move the claim from the immediate delay to its supposed long-run result.
The future ending -á states the promised later result and carries the written accent.
Nos identifies the people who benefit, ahorrará gives the future saving action, and tiempo names what is saved.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone passes or hands an object to another person?
cards.answerEn: Use pasar for the handing action, name the object, and identify the recipient with a short word such as me or te, or with a + person.
cards.noteEn: The short recipient word normally comes before a changed form of pasar, as in me pasas, or attaches to an unchanged infinitive, as in pasarte. The object is the thing being handed.

cards.promptEs: pasar la sal · sistema · condimentos arbitrarios · ahorrar tiempo
cards.questionEn: Why does the promised time-saving system make the exchange absurd?
cards.answerEn: A simple request to pass the salt is delayed while the listener builds a general-purpose condiment-passing system.
cards.noteEn: The joke contrasts solving one immediate task with overengineering a reusable solution. The official title text extends the contrast by showing how present-day thoroughness can look like poor prioritization while similar past work is praised as craftsmanship.
Pasas is the familiar singular present form of pasar. With a recipient word such as me and an object, it means passing or handing that object to the listener.

example.en: Could you pass me the water?

cards.noteEn: Sal is the feminine noun for salt. Do not confuse it with sal, the informal command of salir meaning ‘leave.’

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Dicho is the irregular completed-action form of decir, “to say.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “said.”
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Desarrollando is the ongoing-action form of desarrollar. It describes a process that is currently being created or improved.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to pass to you; to hand to you
cards.noteEn: Pasarte combines the unchanged dictionary form pasar with te, which identifies one familiar listener as the recipient.

example.en: I am going to pass you the report.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.
Condimentos is the plural of condimento, a seasoning or table condiment added to food.

example.es: Hay varios condimentos en la mesa.
example.en: There are several condiments on the table.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: arbitrary; unrestricted by a fixed choice
cards.noteEn: Arbitrarios is masculine plural to match a masculine plural noun. It describes choices that are not limited to one predetermined case.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an amount of time passes or has elapsed?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of pasar followed by the amount of time.
cards.noteEn: The time amount acts as the subject: pasó una hora, pasaron dos días, or han pasado veinte minutos. This is different from pasar tiempo haciendo algo, which means spending time on an activity.
Pasado is the completed-action form of pasar. With a form of haber and a duration, it says that an amount of time has gone by.

cards.answerEn: in; begins a la larga, ‘in the long run’
cards.noteEn: A is the first fixed part of a la larga. Its English meaning is supplied by the whole expression.

example.es: A la larga, la práctica ayuda.
example.en: In the long run, practice helps.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘in the long run’?
cards.noteEn: A la larga looks beyond the immediate situation to the eventual result over time.

example.es: A la larga, el cambio será útil.
example.en: In the long run, the change will be useful.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of a la larga
cards.noteEn: La is fixed between a and larga in the expression a la larga, ‘in the long run.’

example.es: A la larga, será más fácil.
example.en: In the long run, it will be easier.

cards.answerEn: long run; completes a la larga
cards.noteEn: Larga completes the fixed expression a la larga. Outside the expression, larga is the feminine form of largo, ‘long.’

example.en: In the long run, we will save money.

cards.noteEn: Before a verb such as salir or resultar, nos can identify the people for whom an outcome is advantageous, costly, easy, or difficult.

example.es: Nos resulta más barato viajar juntos.
example.en: It works out cheaper for us to travel together.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something saves someone time?
cards.answerEn: Use a short beneficiary word such as me, te, le, nos, os, or les with ahorrar, followed by tiempo.
cards.noteEn: The short word identifies who benefits: me ahorra tiempo, nos ahorrará tiempo, and so on. A phrase beginning with a may name that beneficiary explicitly.
Ahorrará is the simple future form of ahorrar for one person or thing. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.
